_comment: Every popover follows the same contract: a plain definition, why it matters here, then a real source. Some words cannot be avoided on this page, so they get explained where they appear rather than assumed.

appeal.title: Appeal
appeal.plain: Asking the agency to look at your case again after it refused some help, and sending papers that answer the reason it gave.
appeal.why: The decision letter starts a 60-day window for this. Missing that window is usually final, which is why the whole product is built around the clock rather than around the paperwork.
appeal.source: FEMA: 8 Tips for Appealing FEMA's Decision

decision-letter.title: Decision letter
decision-letter.plain: The letter the agency sends telling you what help was approved or refused, and why.
decision-letter.why: This letter, not a general checklist, decides which documents actually matter for your case. Sixty Days reads your letter and follows what it says, quoting it word for word.
decision-letter.source: FEMA: the letter explains the reason and the documents

reminder.title: Reminder
reminder.plain: A date the system sets for itself in advance, so it can come back and do something on that day without being asked.
reminder.why: Eight of them are set the moment a case opens, running from day 3 to day 58. That is what makes this different from a chat window: it keeps working while you are doing something else.
reminder.source: FEMA: Individual Assistance Appeals Quick Reference

simulated-clock.title: Simulated clock
simulated-clock.plain: A pretend calendar for the demonstration, so you can jump forward weeks in seconds instead of waiting two months.
simulated-clock.why: The reminders are real and so is the code that runs them. Only the date is fast-forwarded, and the page always says when you are looking at pretend time. The live service is also woken by a real scheduler every minute on the real clock.

draft-packet.title: Draft packet
draft-packet.plain: A PDF that gathers the letter's reasons, whatever documents have been collected, and a clear list of what is still missing.
draft-packet.why: It is a draft on purpose. It is not an official form, it is not filed anywhere, and it never hides a gap by leaving it out. You read it and decide what to do.
draft-packet.source: FEMA: an appeal letter or form is optional

ready-for-review.title: Ready for your review
ready-for-review.plain: The photo is clear enough and shows enough of the scene that it is worth you looking at it.
ready-for-review.why: It is deliberately not the same as 'accepted', 'genuine', or 'enough'. The system only checks whether a picture is readable and wide enough. It cannot judge whether damage is disaster-related, what it is worth, or what an agency will accept.
ready-for-review.source: FEMA: how records and evidence are verified

synthetic.title: Made up for the demo
synthetic.plain: Every letter, photo, name, address, and case number on this site was invented for the demonstration.
synthetic.why: No real survivor's information is used anywhere, so you can click every button freely. It also means the accuracy numbers describe these invented examples, not a promise about your own letter.
